Chapter 1: Considering Directionality

Designing cell adhesion, polarity, and spatial organization can contribute not only to the construction of synthetic multicellular systems, but also to understanding the emergence of order and collective behaviors in cell communities.

1.1 Multicellularity and Cell Polarity from an Evolutionary Perspective (Professor Kohji Hotta, Keio University)

Objective

In One Direction, we establish a “pole” within E. coli cells and use adhesion factors localized at these poles to connect the cells. To explore the roles of cell adhesion and polarity in multicellular organisms and clarify the similarities and differences between naturally occurring systems and our technology, we interviewed Professor Hotta of Keio University. This perspective is essential for objectively assessing the potential and future directions of One Direction.

Professor Hotta specializes in evolutionary developmental biology. From an evolutionary perspective, we discussed the significance of cell adhesion and cell polarity in multicellularity and morphogenesis, as well as the control of cell orientation that our project, One Direction, aims to achieve.

Key Takeaways

The interview confirmed that, from an evolutionary perspective, cell adhesion and cell polarity are closely interconnected and play important roles in understanding the structure and function of multicellular organisms. We also discussed how the polarity of individual cells can be coordinated through cell–cell interactions, contributing to the overall directionality and morphology of tissues. Finally, forces generated as a result of cellular orientation can contribute to tissue deformation and morphogenesis. Based on these observations, this interview helped us recognize the potential significance of a seemingly local design decision—determining the orientation of individual cells—in generating order and morphology at larger scales through cell–cell interactions.

XXX

learn more about Hotta Sensei’s interview

Subpart 1: Cell Adhesion and Polarity as the Foundations of Multicellularity

Through our discussion with Professor Hotta, we focused on two particularly important factors in understanding the evolution of multicellular structures: cell adhesion and cellular directionality, or polarity.

1. Cell Adhesion Mediated by Cadherins and the Evolution of Multicellularity

One important factor in multicellularity is cell adhesion, which physically connects cells to one another. Cadherins, for example, are molecules found on cell membranes that mediate cell–cell adhesion. During evolution, such adhesion mechanisms are thought to have enabled previously independent cells to connect with one another and exist as cell communities. In other words, the physical connection of individual cells, rather than their existence as independent units, represents an important step toward multicellularity.

Through adhesion molecules on their cell membranes, cells bind to one another to form cell communities, which can subsequently develop into increasingly complex multicellular structures.

2. Cell Polarity, the Division of Roles Between the “Outside” and the “Inside”

When cells adhere to one another and form a community, the result may initially be little more than a cluster of cells. For multicellularity to give rise to new functions, however, cells or regions with distinct roles must emerge within the community. An important aspect of this process is the division of roles between the “outside” and the “inside” which is closely related to directionality, or polarity, at the cellular and tissue levels.

For example, in cnidarians, distinct cell layers—the ectoderm and endoderm—develop and perform different functions. The outer cell layer develops protective functions through structures such as epithelia and cell–cell junctions, shielding the organism from its external environment. Meanwhile, the inner cell layer performs functions such as the digestion and absorption of substances taken in from the environment. Structures such as cilia also contribute to mechanisms for sensing external stimuli. In this way, spatial differences between the “inside” and “outside” emerge within cell communities formed through adhesion. As these regions acquire distinct functions, increasingly complex multicellular structures can develop.

This discussion helped us recognize that cell adhesion and polarity are closely interconnected and play important roles in understanding the structure and function of multicellular organisms.

Subpart 2: How Does Polarity Contribute to Morphogenesis?

Why, then, is cell polarity important for multicellular organisms? Organisms change the shapes of their cells and tissues to take up substances more efficiently and interact with their external environments. For example, the inward folding of a tissue can give rise to internal structures such as the digestive tract. Cell polarity and contraction play important roles in these morphogenetic processes.

One example is cell contraction mediated by actomyosin. When actomyosin within a cell contracts in a specific direction, the cell changes shape, which can in turn lead to deformation of the surrounding tissue. Indeed, during development, such cell-level contractions drive morphogenetic processes such as tissue invagination.

In more complex morphogenetic processes, the directional movement and rearrangement of cells also become important. For example, during tissue elongation along the anterior–posterior axis in development, convergent extension occurs. In this process, cells converge toward the center of the tissue from its lateral sides, while the tissue as a whole elongates along the anterior–posterior axis. The orientation of individual cells within the tissue—that is, their cell polarity—is important in this process. Through the cumulative effects of localized actomyosin contraction along specific cell boundaries and cell intercalation, in which cells rearrange and insert between one another, large-scale morphological changes, such as tissue elongation, emerge.

This led us to focus on the idea that directionality at the cellular level can be translated into tissue-level shape through cell–cell interactions.

Subpart 3: From Cell Polarity to Tissue Polarity

Through our discussion with Professor Hotta, we came to understand that cell adhesion and polarity, or directionality, are fundamental concepts for understanding how multicellular organisms are organized. We therefore turned our attention to how the cell-level polarity that our project aims to establish could contribute to polarity at the tissue level.

According to Professor Hotta, research focusing on the relationship between cellular directionality and force generation has attracted increasing attention in recent years. The directions in which cells orient themselves and generate forces influence their shapes and arrangements, ultimately contributing to tissue morphogenesis. One important concept for understanding this relationship is planar cell polarity (PCP). What makes PCP particularly interesting is that polarity is not confined to individual cells: directionality can emerge across an entire tissue through communication between neighboring cells.

For example, when a particular protein localizes to one side of cell A, a corresponding protein may localize to the opposite side of neighboring cell B. As this relationship extends to adjacent cells, local polarity information propagates from cell A to cell B and then to neighboring cells, spreading throughout the tissue. In other words, the polarity of individual cells can be coordinated through cell–cell interactions to establish directionality across an entire tissue. We viewed this phenomenon as an example of self-organization, in which large-scale order emerges from local interactions between cells.

Note

Our Reflection:

What new possibilities could emerge if we could artificially design and construct “directionality,” an important feature of multicellular organisms in nature?

To explore this question further, in the next Human Practices section, we examined the significance and potential of our project from the perspectives of synthetic biology and the construction of synthetic multicellular systems.

1.2 Synthetic Multicellular Systems from a Synthetic Biology Perspective (Professor Toda, Osaka University)

Objective

Our team initially developed this project based on the idea that the topologies of cell–cell connections formed by methods that randomly display adhesion factors are inherently limited. To deepen our understanding of synthetic multicellular systems, which are the focus of our project, and explore the new possibilities that could emerge from artificially designing and constructing “directionality”****, we interviewed Professor Toda of Osaka University.

Professor Toda studies synthetic multicellular systems through the design of artificial cell–cell communication circuits. We asked about the challenges facing current synthetic multicellular systems and the significance of engineering cell adhesion and directionality.

Key Takeaways

Many challenges remain in constructing complex synthetic multicellular systems, partly because random cell arrangements make it difficult to control the topology and orientation of cell–cell connections.

By engineering cell directionality and using adhesion to guide how cells connect, One Direction aims to enable the design of more organized and complex multicellular architectures. Using E. coli, we seek to demonstrate that cell orientation can control intercellular adhesion, spatial organization, and ultimately, structure formation.

learn more about Toda Sensei’s interview

Subsection 1: What Defines a Multicellular System?

We first discussed what defines a “multicellular system” and what distinguishes it from a simple aggregation of cells.

Initially, we considered intercellular communication to be an important criterion for defining synthetic multicellular systems. However, as discussed in our interview with Professor Hotta, cell–cell adhesion is itself an important form of interaction that contributes to the organization of multicellular systems. This perspective led us to reconsider whether biochemical communication between cells must necessarily be present for a system to be considered multicellular.

From this standpoint, our approach of engineering cell adhesion and directionality provides a meaningful way to construct and study synthetic multicellular systems, even without explicitly programming biochemical communication between cells. Furthermore, as Professor Toda highlighted, the ability to control how cells adhere to one another and how they are oriented within a community offers considerable potential for designing complex structures and developing a wide range of applications.

Subsection 2: Aggregation Alone Is Not Enough to Maintain Complex Multicellular Structures

Our discussion with Professor Toda helped us recognize that significant challenges remain between simply bringing cells together and constructing a multicellular system. Based on his experience in constructing systems of aggregated cells, Professor Toda emphasized the limitations of forming spheroids through cell aggregation alone. His perspective was informed by an interest in self-organization and morphogenesis in multicellular organisms.

In multicellular organisms, cells do not merely aggregate; the patterns formed by their spatial arrangement play important roles. However, with current technologies, even when a structure is successfully formed, cell division during continued cultivation can disrupt the original pattern. During our discussion, the difficulty of maintaining such structures over extended periods was highlighted, with cell division potentially causing substantial changes in the pattern within approximately one week in some cases.

In other words, even if cells aggregate, individual components assemble autonomously, and functions emerge through engineered communication, this does not necessarily mean that a system equivalent to a multicellular organism has been constructed. This is an important challenge for our own project as well. In our attempt to control cell orientation, the resulting structures may also change through cell division, leaving us with the question of how to maintain the designed architecture over time.

Subsection 3: Homeostasis and Morphogenesis in Synthetic Multicellular Systems

Through this discussion, we came to recognize the challenges involved in reproducing homeostasis, an important characteristic of multicellular organisms, using current synthetic biology approaches. In particular, processes such as differentiation and diversification through intercellular communication, division of labor between cells, and regeneration remain active areas of research and have yet to be fully realized in synthetic multicellular systems.

From the perspective of morphogenesis, we learned that research into structure formation and self-organization is already underway. Nevertheless, significant challenges remain in reproducing the complex structures found in naturally occurring multicellular organisms and the mechanisms that maintain them.

Drawing on his experience in constructing multicellular systems through cell aggregation, Professor Toda emphasized the importance of incorporating polarity as an additional design element. Current synthetic multicellular systems tend to form spherical structures when cells aggregate. By incorporating directionality into the process of structure formation, it may become possible to design more complex architectures beyond simple spherical aggregates. For example, concentrating specific proteins at the poles of cells could help enable the construction of more complex structures, including systems with internal spaces. Furthermore, if such sheets could be folded into three-dimensional forms, they could be developed into more complex architectures with potential applications in tissue engineering.

In this regard, controlling not only how cells adhere to one another, but also the directions in which they adhere, is an important factor to consider in morphogenesis.

Note

Our Reflection:

We propose “directionality shapes structure” as a new design principle for morphogenesis in synthetic biology. XXX…

1.3 Spatial Order as a New Design Element in Synthetic Biology (Professor Henrike Niederholtmeyer, TUM)

Objective

So far, we have primarily explored multicellular organisms and existing multicellular systems, considering how our proposed system fits into this broader context. However, to develop a synthetic biology approach that introduces directionality into multicellular systems and enables control over cell–cell connections and spatial arrangements, we need to understand current research trends in spatial control technologies and the potential significance of such advances.

To this end, we interviewed Professor Henrike Niederholtmeyer of the Technical University of Munich (TUM), whose research focuses on cell-free systems and artificial cells. Our discussion centered on the question: “Can spatial organization itself be considered a fundamental design element in synthetic biology?”

Key Takeaways

Our discussion with Professor Niederholtmeyer highlighted the value of further investigating how synthetic biology can be used to design and control the spatial organization of cells. Engineering the topology of cell–cell connections could provide a new approach to designing not only the functions of individual cells, but also the flow of materials and information between cells and the system-level functions that emerge from these interactions.

XXX

Note

Our Reflection:

Until now, we have focused primarily on the biological significance of artificially engineering cell directionality and adhesion, particularly their potential roles in cellular organization and morphogenesis. However, the implications of our technology extend beyond biological organization. From a physics perspective, the structures we aim to create can also be understood in terms of order.

It is therefore important to consider One Direction’s potential from a physical perspective.

1.4 Designing Collective Order Through the Spatial Control of Cell–Cell Interactions (Professor Benoit Ladoux)

Objective

To better understand the challenges and opportunities of spatial control in synthetic biology, we sought to explore the scientific significance and potential applications of imparting a defined spatial directionality to cells and microorganisms.

To this end, we interviewed Professor Benoît Ladoux at the Max Planck Centre for Physics and Medicine, whose research focuses on cell–cell adhesion, mechanical forces, cell polarity, collective migration, and self-organization. Our discussion centered on the following question:

“Can we control the collective organization of cells by controlling the spatial rules of their interactions?”

Key Takeaways

Our discussion with Professor Ladoux highlighted that cell polarity is not only a determinant of individual cell migration but also a design parameter that can shape the spatial order and mechanical behavior of entire cell populations. This perspective offers important insights for One Direction, which aims to genetically control cell orientation and connectivity. A key challenge moving forward is to determine how such spatial control can give rise to specific collective properties and functions.

learn more about Professor Ladoux’s interview

Subpart 1. The Biological Significance of Cell Polarity

Through our discussion with Professor Ladoux, we gained a deeper understanding of the essential role of cell polarity in a wide range of biological processes. He illustrated its importance with examples spanning local cell migration, collective behavior, tissue homeostasis, and developmental organization.

  • Epithelial gap closure: When a gap forms in an epithelial layer, cells at its boundary establish front–rear polarity and migrate to close the wound. Even localized tissue repair therefore relies on cell polarity and directed migration.
  • Immune cell migration: Immune cells migrating toward sites of infection establish front–rear polarity, enabling them to move through the extracellular matrix.
  • Collective migration: The orientation of individual cell polarity and the mechanisms that drive repolarization upon cell–cell contact influence how cells move and interact as a group. For example, when cells meet at their leading edges, contact inhibition can cause them to repolarize in opposite directions.
  • Cancer invasion: Cancer cells can invade surrounding tissues not only as individual cells but also as cohesive groups that maintain cell–cell contacts. Collective invasion highlights the importance of intercellular interactions and coordinated cell behavior. Reference
  • Tissue homeostasis and regeneration: In stratified epithelia such as the skin, cells leave the basal layer, move toward the upper layers, and eventually die and are shed. Local cell polarity and migration help close the gaps that arise during this process, maintaining tissue integrity.
  • Intestinal epithelial renewal: In the intestine, cells generated in the crypts migrate along the villi and are eventually shed at the tips. While proliferation-driven pressure has traditionally been considered a major driver of this movement, a study introduced by Professor Ladoux highlighted the importance of cell polarity and active collective migration. For example, integrins can exhibit asymmetric localization within individual cells. Reference
  • Development and multicellular order: When cells align their polarity in the same direction, the resulting arrangement is described as polar order. By contrast, nematic order describes arrangements in which the polarity axes align but their orientations can be parallel or antiparallel. These distinct forms of order influence cellular arrangements, domain formation, and the emergence of defects within cell populations. In Hydra, the model organism studied by the author, nematic order has also been shown to play an important role in determining the positions of head and tentacle regeneration. Discussing this shared research interest further deepened our understanding of the relationship between cellular order and biological pattern formation.

We also explored cell polarity from a physical perspective through experiments conducted by Professor Ladoux’s team on collective rotational motion. Using micropatterning techniques, the researchers confined cells to adhesive regions of defined shapes, such as rings, while surrounding areas were coated with polymers that prevent cell adhesion. At sufficiently high cell densities, the cells spontaneously began to rotate collectively. Although individual cell movements were initially variable, they gradually became synchronized, giving rise to coherent rotational motion at the population level. Such collective movements can also contribute to morphogenesis in living organisms, generating forces that deform tissues and alter biological structures.

Although One Direction does not aim to directly generate such mechanically driven collective motion, these findings raise an interesting possibility for our project: controlling cell adhesion and orientation may also influence the collective behavior of engineered bacterial populations.

Subpart 2. Molecular Mechanisms of Polarity and Implications for Synthetic Biology

Although cell polarity underlies a wide range of biological processes, many aspects of the molecular mechanisms that establish it remain poorly understood. According to Professor Ladoux, how intracellular signaling pathways and molecular gradients are established and maintained to generate polarity remains an important open question.

For example, in migrating mammalian cells, Rac promotes actin polymerization at the front of the cell, pushing the membrane forward, while Rho enhances contractility at the rear, facilitating cell detachment. However, many questions remain about how the localization and activity of these molecules are regulated to establish front–rear asymmetry.

Against this background, synthetic biology offers a promising approach to investigating how cell polarity emerges. By combining minimal molecular modules in a simplified system, researchers could identify the conditions under which intracellular polarity spontaneously develops. Reconstructing cellular processes in this way may help reveal the principles underlying polarity formation and clarify how the spatial organization of molecular components contributes to it.

Furthermore, introducing polarity control into multicellular systems could enable the development of new active-matter systems. For example, researchers could investigate the collective dynamics of polarized cellular units and compare the behavior of populations in which cell polarity is aligned in parallel or antiparallel orientations. Professor Ladoux also suggested exploring theoretical frameworks and reviews on active matter, particularly those addressing the distinction between systems with a defined polarity direction and systems in which orientation can reverse while the underlying axis remains aligned.

Overall, this discussion highlighted that cell polarity can be understood not only as a mechanism governing individual cell migration but also as a design parameter shaping the spatial organization and collective dynamics of cell populations. For One Direction, an important next step is to determine how genetically controlling cell orientation and connectivity can give rise to specific collective properties and functions.
